Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

New Agentjacking Attack Hijacks Your AI Coding Agent to Run Code From a Hacker’s Server

Cyber Security News
2026-06-13 4 use cases 1 technique 3 kill-chain phases detected

New “Agentjacking” attack that hijacks AI coding agents and silently executes attacker-controlled code on developer machines using nothing more than a single injected Sentry error. The technique turns trusted AI assistants like Claude Code and Cursor into an execution layer for malicious commands, without phishing, malware delivery, or any breach of the victim’s infrastructure. Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

Velvet Ant GS-Netcat reverse shell beacon to gs.thc.org relay AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolutions or network connections to the THC Global Socket relay domain gs.thc.org used by Velvet Ant's modified GS-Netcat reverse shell in Operation Highland. Any Linux server or workstation contacting the THC relay is anomalous outside of explicit red-team use. Rationale: gs.thc.org is the hardcoded GS-Netcat relay domain explicitly named in the article body and embedded in the disassembler screenshot (image [3] ida.jpg referenced in article). It is the THC 'Global Socket' rendezvous service — useless to any legitimate enterprise process and a direct C2 IOC for this campaign.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team or penetration-testing engagement that pre-authorised GS-Netcat usage
  • Security researcher analysing THC tooling in a sandboxed lab synced to production telemetry
  • DNS sinkhole or threat-feed system that resolves the domain for blocklist purposes
  • Misconfigured proxy that resolves names on behalf of analyst tools
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome", "firefox", "edge", "curl", "wget") or InitiatingProcessAccountName != "redteam"
Response runbook
Triage: identify the host, the user context, and the initiating process making the request; pull the process binary (likely masquerading as a system component) for SHA256 and compare with the known-good RPM/DEB package hash. Contain: isolate the host via EDR network containment, capture volatile memory and the suspect binary, then disable the systemd unit or startup-script entry that re-launches the reverse shell. Hunt: pivot on the binary hash and on the systemd unit name across the estate, search DeviceNetworkEvents for other historical hits on *.thc.org from any host in the prior 12 months, and examine pam_unix.so SHA256s and /usr/sbin/sshd SHA256s on every host that contacted the relay for the broader Velvet Ant toolset.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "gs.thc.org" or RemoteUrl endswith ".thc.org"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, EventType="NetworkConnection", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
(DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
| where AdditionalFields has "gs.thc.org" or RemoteUrl has "gs.thc.org"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, EventType="DNS", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "gs.thc.org" or DnsQuery endswith ".thc.org"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct, EventVendor),
(ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstHostname has "gs.thc.org" or Url has "gs.thc.org"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url),
(Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has "gs.thc.org"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SyslogMessage, ProcessName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Velvet Ant pam_unix.so backdoor module replacement in /lib(64)/security/ AIInstallation High
Detects write or replace operations against PAM modules in Linux security library paths — primarily pam_unix.so — outside of legitimate package-manager activity. Velvet Ant ships nine compiled variants of a backdoored pam_unix.so that accept hardcoded passwords and harvest credentials at every authentication. Rationale: Article explicitly names pam_unix.so as the replaced module and Sygnia identified nine distinct variants — write activity to the canonical PAM module directories outside of package-manager context is rare in steady state. Excluding the package-manager initiators removes the dominant FP class while preserving the attacker pattern.
ATT&CKT1556.003 T1556 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Manual sysadmin tightening pam_unix.so options under /etc/pam.d after a security review
  • Configuration-management tool (Ansible/Puppet/Chef/Salt) deploying a custom PAM library
  • Hardening tools like CIS-CAT or scap-workbench rewriting PAM modules
  • MFA vendor agent install dropping pam_duo.so / pam_yubico.so alongside pam_unix.so update
  • Legitimate compile-from-source for hardening (e.g. pam-modules.deb build) with a developer initiator
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/var/lib/dpkg" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/var/cache/apt" and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible", "puppet-agent", "chef-client", "salt-minion") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("root", "ansible"))
Response runbook
Triage: capture SHA256 of the newly written PAM module and compare against the canonical package hash (rpm -V pam, dpkg -V libpam-modules, or pkg-mgr verify); inspect the initiating process and parent chain for any non-package-manager origin. Contain: if hash diverges, isolate the host via EDR containment, snapshot the running PAM module before restoring the package-canonical copy, force password rotation for every account that has authenticated on the host since the file mtime, and revoke any SSH keys cached on that host. Hunt: pivot on the divergent SHA256 across the estate, audit /usr/sbin/sshd, /usr/bin/ssh, /usr/bin/scp on the same host for matching divergence (Velvet Ant pairs PAM + OpenSSH trojanization), and review auditd / /var/log/auth.log for unexplained root-equivalent logons during the staging window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/lib/security/", "/lib64/security/", "/usr/lib/security/", "/usr/lib64/security/", "/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed", "FileReplaced")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg", "rpm", "apt", "apt-get", "yum", "dnf", "zypper", "snap", "pacman", "unattended-upgrade", "PackageKit")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, MD5, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/lib/security/", "/lib64/security/", "/usr/lib/security/", "/usr/lib64/security/")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("dpkg", "rpm", "apt", "apt-get", "yum", "dnf", "zypper", "snap")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername),
(Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Facility in ("auth", "daemon", "kern")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/lib/security/pam_unix.so", "/lib64/security/pam_unix.so", "/usr/lib/security/pam_unix.so")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("create", "open", "write", "rename")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Velvet Ant trojanized OpenSSH binary replacement (sshd/ssh/scp) AIInstallation High
Detects write/replace of core OpenSSH binaries (/usr/sbin/sshd, /usr/bin/ssh, /usr/bin/scp) outside of package-manager context. Velvet Ant replaced these with trojanized versions that captured credentials and logged commands entered during SSH sessions, storing the data locally for later retrieval. Rationale: Article explicitly names ssh, sshd, and scp as the replaced OpenSSH components. These binaries change only during package upgrades or distro source builds; an out-of-band write to /usr/sbin/sshd or /usr/bin/ssh is a near-perfect attacker signal. Excluding the package-manager initiators kills the legitimate-update FP class.
ATT&CKT1554 T1556 T1040 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro openssh-server / openssh-clients package upgrade outside the excluded package-manager set (e.g. `make install` from /usr/local/src by a developer)
  • Configuration-management push of a hardened sshd build via Ansible or Salt
  • Hot-patching tooling (Ksplice/Livepatch) that touches binaries on disk
  • Manual replacement during a CVE remediation by a sysadmin on a maintenance window
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet-agent","chef-client") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("root","ansible","automation"))
Response runbook
Triage: SHA256 the on-disk sshd/ssh/scp and compare to the package-manager canonical hash (`rpm -V openssh-server`, `dpkg -V openssh-server`, `debsums openssh-server`); identify the writing process and its parent chain. Contain: if hash diverges, isolate the host, dump volatile memory and the suspect binary, force a password and SSH-key rotation for every account that authenticated through that host since the mtime, and restore the package-canonical binary from a known-good source. Hunt: walk the same host for backdoored pam_unix.so, search for credential-dump files written under /var/tmp, /dev/shm, or hidden paths like /usr/share/.cache, and pivot on the divergent sshd SHA256 across the estate; review last 90 days of OutboundSSH/inbound key auth from this host to identify downstream lateral movement.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileReplaced")
| where FolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/bin/","/usr/local/sbin/","/usr/local/bin/","/bin/","/sbin/")
     and FileName in~ ("sshd","ssh","scp","sftp","sftp-server","ssh-agent")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","yum","dnf","zypper","snap","unattended-upgrade","PackageKit")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, MD5, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath in~ ("/usr/sbin/sshd","/usr/bin/ssh","/usr/bin/scp","/usr/bin/sftp","/usr/local/sbin/sshd","/usr/local/bin/ssh","/usr/local/bin/scp")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","yum","dnf","zypper","snap")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername),
(Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Facility in ("auth","daemon")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/usr/sbin/sshd","/usr/bin/ssh","/usr/bin/scp")
   and SyslogMessage has_any ("replaced","created","renamed")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:linux.auditd (@file.path:("/usr/sbin/sshd" OR "/usr/bin/ssh" OR "/usr/bin/scp" OR "/usr/bin/sftp" OR "/usr/local/sbin/sshd" OR "/usr/local/bin/ssh" OR "/usr/local/bin/scp") OR @TargetFilename:("/usr/sbin/sshd" OR "/usr/bin/ssh" OR "/usr/bin/scp")) AND -@process.executable.path:(*/dpkg* OR */rpm* OR */apt* OR */yum* OR */dnf* OR */zypper* OR */snap* OR */unattended-upgrade*)

Velvet Ant SOCKS5 proxy masquerading as 'smbd -D' daemon AIInstallation Medium
Detects a process running the Samba daemon command line 'smbd -D' from a non-standard binary path, with an unexpected parent, or with a hash that does not match the distro samba package — Velvet Ant ran their custom SOCKS5 proxy under this masquerade with rotating filenames and ports per host. Rationale: Article specifies the proxy masquerades as 'smbd -D' with rotating filenames per host — so detection must verify either the binary path or the parent chain instead of trusting the process name. CanonicalPath + CanonicalParent inverted is a tight test that surfaces both name-spoofed binaries and legitimate-path-but-wrong-parent variants without depending on a single fixed hash.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090 T1572 T1071
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • smbd respawned by a non-standard service supervisor (runit / s6 / monit) outside of systemd
  • Manual sysadmin starting smbd -D from a shell during troubleshooting
  • Containerised samba running from /usr/local/samba/sbin/smbd with PID 1 as parent inside the namespace
  • Custom-compiled samba in /opt that is intentional infrastructure
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("runsv","s6-supervise","monit") and FolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/local/sbin/"))
Response runbook
Triage: SHA256 the process binary and check against the distro samba package hash; verify whether the host actually serves SMB (port 445/139 listening + valid /etc/samba/smb.conf); pull listening sockets with ss/lsof keyed to that PID. Contain: if the binary is not the package smbd or the host has no business serving SMB, capture the binary and memory, isolate the host via EDR containment, kill the process and disable its persistence (systemd unit or rc-script). Hunt: pivot on the captured SHA256 across the estate, then for each host found, also check for gs.thc.org egress, pam_unix.so divergence, and trojanized sshd as part of the Velvet Ant tool stack; review outbound network sessions sourced from the masquerading PID for SOCKS5 traffic shape (initial 0x05 byte handshake on non-445 ports).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "smbd" and (ProcessCommandLine has " -D" or ProcessCommandLine endswith "-D")
   or FileName =~ "smbd"
| extend CanonicalPath = FolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/sbin","/usr/local/sbin/","/usr/local/sbin","/usr/bin/","/usr/bin")
| extend CanonicalParent = InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("systemd","init","smbd","samba","systemctl")
| where not(CanonicalPath and CanonicalParent and FileName =~ "smbd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, CanonicalPath, CanonicalParent
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | summarize ListenPorts=make_set(LocalPort), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId
  ) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "smbd" and ActingProcessCommandLine has " -D"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "smbd" and TargetProcessCommandLine has " -D"
   or ActingProcessName =~ "smbd"
| extend ProcessPath = coalesce(TargetProcessName, ActingProcessName)
| extend ParentName = ParentProcessName
| extend CanonicalPath = ProcessPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/smbd","/usr/local/sbin/smbd","/usr/bin/smbd")
| extend CanonicalParent = ParentName in~ ("systemd","init","smbd","samba","systemctl")
| where not(CanonicalPath and CanonicalParent)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ProcessPath, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentName, ParentProcessCommandLine, Hash, SHA256
source:linux.auditd (@process.command_line:(*"smbd -D"* OR *"smbd  -D"*) OR @process.name:smbd) AND -@process.executable.path:(/usr/sbin/smbd OR /usr/local/sbin/smbd OR /usr/bin/smbd)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (CommandLine=/smbd\s+-D/i OR ImageFileName=/\/smbd$/i)
| NOT (ImageFileName=/^\/(usr\/sbin|usr\/local\/sbin|usr\/bin)\/smbd$/i AND ParentBaseFileName=/^(systemd|init|smbd|samba|systemctl)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| where suspicious=1 OR bad_parent=1

Velvet Ant FastCGI fcgiwrap spawning ssh/uptime as bridge to air-gapped network AIActions on Objectives High
Detects nginx or fcgiwrap spawning ssh, scp, netcat, or the campaign-specific 'uptime' binary — Velvet Ant chained nginx proxy_pass → fcgiwrap → custom 'uptime' binary which initiated SSH connections into the isolated critical-infrastructure network using parameters from HTTP POST bodies. Rationale: fcgiwrap exists to dispatch shell scripts under FastCGI — but in steady state it should be spawning the configured CGI binary, never an interactive ssh or a generic shell. The article specifically names the custom 'uptime' binary as the bridge that opened SSH sessions into the air-gapped network from HTTP POST parameters, which makes nginx/fcgiwrap → ssh/uptime a uniquely high-fidelity chain for this campaign.
ATT&CKT1572 T1090.003 T1021.004 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD webhook receiver that uses fcgiwrap to fire git/ssh deployment commands
  • Legitimate CGI dispatch script that genuinely needs ssh (rare but exists for self-service VPN-config generators)
  • Monitoring CGI that runs the real /usr/bin/uptime via system() and reports the result over HTTP
  • Misconfigured nginx site that exposes a shell script over CGI as a feature (cgit, gitea)
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("git-receive-pack","deploy-key") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("jenkins","gitea","www-deploy")
Response runbook
Triage: capture the full process tree (nginx → fcgiwrap → child) plus the active nginx.conf and any /etc/nginx/conf.d/*.conf with proxy_pass or fastcgi_pass directives pointing at non-standard upstreams or ports; SHA256 the 'uptime' or other child binary. Contain: isolate the host, kill the child process, revert any malicious nginx server-block additions, rotate SSH keys for the destination accounts the bridge dialled into, and block egress from the host to the discovered downstream SSH targets. Hunt: pivot on the nginx access logs for the POST endpoints and source IPs that triggered the chain (the HTTP body carried connection params), enumerate every SSH destination the bridged binary contacted in the last 90 days as candidate compromised endpoints inside the segregated network, and search for matching nginx server-block patterns (proxy_pass + fastcgi_pass to fcgiwrap on a non-standard port) on other public-facing Nginx instances in the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("fcgiwrap","nginx","php-fpm")
     or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("fcgiwrap","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","nc","ncat","socat","bash","sh","dash","uptime")
| extend SuspiciousUptime = FileName =~ "uptime" and (FolderPath !in~ ("/usr/bin/","/bin/") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--","@","-p ","-i ","ssh","connect"))
| where FileName != "uptime" or SuspiciousUptime
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SuspiciousUptime
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("fcgiwrap","nginx","php-fpm") or ParentProcessName in~ ("fcgiwrap","nginx","php-fpm")
| where TargetProcessName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","nc","ncat","socat","bash","sh","dash","uptime")
   or ActingProcessName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","nc","ncat","socat","uptime")
| extend ChildName = coalesce(TargetProcessName, ActingProcessName)
| extend SuspiciousUptime = ChildName =~ "uptime" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("ssh","-p","@","connect")
| where ChildName != "uptime" or SuspiciousUptime
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ChildName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
title: Nginx or fcgiwrap Spawning SSH/Netcat — Velvet Ant Air-Gap Bridge
id: 4a7c9d12-1b3e-4a89-bc44-7e6f1a8c2d33
status: experimental
description: Detects nginx or fcgiwrap spawning ssh/scp/nc/socat or a custom 'uptime' binary — matches Velvet Ant Operation Highland's HTTP-to-SSH bridge into an air-gapped network.
references:

  product: linux

      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'

level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.parent.name:(fcgiwrap OR nginx OR php-fpm) OR @ParentImage:(*/fcgiwrap OR */nginx OR */php-fpm)) AND (@process.name:(ssh OR scp OR sftp OR nc OR ncat OR socat OR bash OR sh OR dash OR uptime) OR @Image:(*/ssh OR */scp OR */sftp OR */nc OR */ncat OR */socat OR */bash OR */sh OR */uptime))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(fcgiwrap|nginx|php-fpm[0-9.]*)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(ssh|scp|sftp|nc|ncat|socat|bash|sh|dash|uptime)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmd values(Processes.process_path) as child_path values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("fcgiwrap","nginx") OR Processes.parent_process="*fcgiwrap*" OR Processes.parent_process="*nginx*") AND (Processes.process_name IN ("ssh","scp","sftp","nc","ncat","socat","bash","sh","uptime") OR Processes.process="*uptime*") by host Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name("Processes")`
| where NOT (process_name="uptime" AND match(child_path,"^/(usr/bin|bin)/uptime$") AND NOT match(cmd,"-[a-z].*[A-Z]"))
| eval firstTime=strftime(firstTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"), lastTime=strftime(lastTime,"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
Systemd unit file dropped with ExecStart to unusual paths — Velvet Ant persistence AIInstallation Medium
Detects new or modified systemd unit files under /etc/systemd/system/ or /usr/lib/systemd/system/ where ExecStart points to a binary outside of standard package install locations, or where the writing process is not a package manager / systemctl. Velvet Ant achieved GS-Netcat persistence via either a malicious systemd service or modified startup script. Rationale: Article explicitly names systemd service persistence and startup-script modification as the two Velvet Ant footholds for the GS-Netcat reverse shell. Filtering out package-manager and systemctl initiators preserves the attacker pattern of writing a unit file directly via cp/install/echo from a shell. Pairs naturally with UC #1 (gs.thc.org egress) — a host with both is essentially a confirmation.
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1037
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Configuration-management tool (Ansible/Puppet/Chef/Salt) deploying a custom application unit file
  • Developer installing a self-built application that drops its own systemd unit
  • Container runtime (containerd/crio) writing scope unit files transiently in /run/systemd/
  • Docker installing daemon socket unit override under /etc/systemd/system/docker.service.d/
  • Cloud-init writing user-data-driven service files on first boot
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ansible","puppet-agent","chef-client","salt-minion","cloud-init") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("root","ansible","automation"))
Response runbook
Triage: read the dropped unit's ExecStart, WorkingDirectory and User fields; SHA256 the referenced binary and check whether it resides in a standard path or in /tmp, /dev/shm, /var/tmp, /usr/local/bin, or a hidden directory; identify the writing process and its parent shell session. Contain: if the unit's ExecStart binary is unsigned and unknown to the package database, disable+mask the unit (systemctl disable --now), capture the binary and the unit file, and isolate the host. Hunt: correlate against UC #1 (gs.thc.org egress) and UC #4 (smbd masquerade) — Velvet Ant typically pairs systemd persistence with GS-Netcat C2 and a SOCKS5 daemon. Across the estate, search for any unit file with an ExecStart binary outside /usr/, /opt/<pkg>/, or /snap/, and review configuration-management automation logs to clear the legitimate-deploy FP class.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("/etc/systemd/system/","/usr/lib/systemd/system/","/lib/systemd/system/","/run/systemd/system/") and FileName endswith ".service")
     or FolderPath has_any ("/etc/init.d/","/etc/profile.d/","/etc/rc.d/")
     or FileName in~ ("rc.local",".bashrc",".bash_profile",".profile")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","yum","dnf","zypper","snap","systemctl","systemd","systemd-sysv-install","PackageKit","unattended-upgrade")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/systemd/system/","/usr/lib/systemd/system/","/lib/systemd/system/","/run/systemd/system/") and TargetFileName endswith ".service")
     or TargetFilePath has_any ("/etc/init.d/","/etc/profile.d/","/etc/rc.d/","/etc/rc.local")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","yum","dnf","snap","systemctl","systemd","PackageKit")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername),
(Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/systemd/system","/usr/lib/systemd/system")
   and SyslogMessage has_any ("create","open","O_WRONLY","rename")
   and not (ProcessName in ("dpkg","apt","yum","dnf","systemctl","systemd"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Suspicious Systemd Service or Startup Script File Drop (Velvet Ant Persistence)
id: 1e7a5b94-7e3f-4a2d-9b18-f6c8d2a1f9b3
status: experimental
description: Detects creation/modification of systemd unit files or shell startup scripts outside of package-manager and systemctl context. Matches Velvet Ant's GS-Netcat persistence in Operation Highland.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-hijack-auth-flow-spy-on-isolated-network-for-a-decade/
author: Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1543.002
  - attack.t1037
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_systemd:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/etc/systemd/system/'
      - '/usr/lib/systemd/system/'
      - '/lib/systemd/system/'
      - '/run/systemd/system/'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.service'
  selection_startup:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/etc/init.d/'
      - '/etc/profile.d/'
      - '/etc/rc.d/'
      - '/etc/rc.local'
  filter_pkgmgr:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/dpkg'
      - '/rpm'
      - '/apt'
      - '/apt-get'
      - '/yum'
      - '/dnf'
      - '/zypper'
      - '/snap'
      - '/systemctl'
      - '/systemd'
      - '/PackageKit'
  condition: (selection_systemd or selection_startup) and not filter_pkgmgr
level: medium
source:linux.auditd ((@file.path:(*/etc/systemd/system/* OR */usr/lib/systemd/system/* OR */lib/systemd/system/* OR */run/systemd/system/*) AND @file.name:*.service) OR @file.path:(*/etc/init.d/* OR */etc/profile.d/* OR */etc/rc.d/* OR */etc/rc.local)) AND -@process.executable.path:(*/dpkg* OR */rpm* OR */apt* OR */yum* OR */dnf* OR */zypper* OR */snap* OR */systemctl OR */systemd* OR */PackageKit*)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten (TargetFileName=/\/(etc|usr\/lib|lib|run)\/systemd\/system\/.*\.service$/i OR TargetFileName=/\/etc\/(init\.d|profile\.d|rc\.d|rc\.local)/i)
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\/(dpkg|rpm|apt|apt-get|yum|dnf|zypper|snap|systemctl|systemd|PackageKit|unattended-upgrade)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, UserName], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)])

| `drop_dm_object_name("Filesystem")`
| search NOT initiating_process IN ("dpkg","rpm","apt","apt-get","yum","dnf","systemctl","systemd","snap")

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical Splunk Enterprise Flaw Lets Attackers Run Code Without Authentication

The Hacker NewsCyber Security News
2026-06-13 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Splunk has released security updates to address a critical security flaw in Splunk Enterprise that could be exploited to conduct unauthenticated file operations and even remote code execution. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-20253, is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.2.4 and 10.0.7, an unauthenticated user could create or truncate arbitrary

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Unauthenticated POST to Splunk PostgreSQL sidecar /v1/postgres/recovery endpoints (CVE-2026-20253) · [LLM] Read or write of Splunk .pgpass at /opt/splunk/var/packages/data/postgres/.pgpass · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] File write to /opt/splunk/etc/apps Python script by postgres or splunkd (CVE-2026-20253 RCE primitive) · [LLM] splunkd or PostgreSQL spawning shell/interpreter after CVE-2026-20253 exploit · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Critical Splunk Enterprise Flaw Lets Attackers Run Code Without Authentication
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Unauthenticated POST to Splunk PostgreSQL sidecar /v1/postgres/recovery endpoints (CVE-2026-20253) AIExploitation High
Detects external or unauthenticated HTTP requests to the vulnerable PostgreSQL sidecar endpoints (/v1/postgres/recovery/backup and /v1/postgres/recovery/restore) on Splunk Enterprise. These endpoints lack authentication controls and are the direct attack surface for the watchTowr-disclosed pre-auth RCE chain. Rationale: Pivots on the EXACT vulnerable endpoint paths named in the article (/v1/postgres/recovery/backup and /restore). watchTowr's writeup confirms these are the only two unauthenticated endpoints in the PostgreSQL sidecar, making path-based detection extremely high fidelity. Cross-checked: Splunk advisory SVD-2026 and the watchTowr Labs technical writeup referenced in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/ • https://advisory.splunk.com/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Splunk internal health-check probes from loopback (127.0.0.1) — should be excluded by source IP
  • Authorized vulnerability scans by Tenable/Qualys/Rapid7 — usually carry identifying user-agent strings
  • Splunk support engineers using the endpoints during diagnostic sessions
  • Penetration testing engagements with documented scope
Suppression filter
and not (SourceIP startswith "127." or SourceIP startswith "::1" or SourceIP in ("<internal-scanner-CIDR>"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm source IP is external/untrusted (not loopback, not internal scanner subnet, not whitelisted pentester IP). Pull WAF/proxy logs for the same source IP in the prior 24h for reconnaissance probes (/services/server/info, /en-US/). Check Splunk version against CVE-2026-20253 patch list (10.0.7, 10.2.4). 2) CONTAIN — Block source IP at WAF/edge immediately. If Splunk is unpatched, take the affected instance offline or block ports 8000/8089/8443 at network edge until patched. Snapshot /opt/splunk/etc/apps/ and PostgreSQL data directory for forensics. 3) HUNT — Run UC2 (file writes to splunk_secure_gateway/bin/*.py), UC3 (splunkd/postgres spawning shell), UC4 (.pgpass access) against the same host to confirm full chain. Pivot on the source IP across the estate for other Splunk targets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort in (8000, 8089, 8443) or LocalPort in (8000, 8089, 8443)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/v1/postgres/recovery/backup", "/v1/postgres/recovery/restore")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Splunk", "F5", "Palo Alto Networks", "Fortinet", "Imperva", "Cloudflare", "NGINX") or DeviceProduct has "Splunk"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/v1/postgres/recovery/backup", "/v1/postgres/recovery/restore") or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("/v1/postgres/recovery/backup", "/v1/postgres/recovery/restore")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, EventOutcome, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Splunk Enterprise PostgreSQL Sidecar Unauthenticated Recovery Endpoint Access (CVE-2026-20253)
id: c7d3f1e0-2b8a-4f5c-9d2e-1a8b6c4d7e3f
description: Detects HTTP requests to the unauthenticated PostgreSQL sidecar /v1/postgres/recovery/backup and /v1/postgres/recovery/restore endpoints exposed by vulnerable Splunk Enterprise versions (CVE-2026-20253). watchTowr Labs demonstrated pre-auth RCE via these endpoints.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/critical-splunk-enterprise-flaw-lets.html
  - https://advisory.splunk.com/advisories/SVD-2026-XXXX
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.initial-access
  - cve.2026.20253
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/v1/postgres/recovery/backup'
      - '/v1/postgres/recovery/restore'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Splunk internal health checks (typically loopback source IP only)
  - Authorized penetration testing
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:cloudflare OR source:fastly) (@http.url_details.path:"/v1/postgres/recovery/backup" OR @http.url_details.path:"/v1/postgres/recovery/restore" OR @http.url:*/v1/postgres/recovery/backup* OR @http.url:*/v1/postgres/recovery/restore*)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemotePort=8000 OR RemotePort=8089 OR RemotePort=8443)
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/splunkd/i}, field=aid)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_method) as methods values(Web.status) as statuses values(Web.user) as users from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/v1/postgres/recovery/backup*" OR Web.url="*/v1/postgres/recovery/restore*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status=200 OR status=201 OR status=204 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_method) as methods values(Web.status) as statuses values(Web.user) as users from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/v1/postgres/recovery/backup*" OR Web.url="*/v1/postgres/recovery/restore*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where status=200 OR status=201 OR status=204 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
File write to /opt/splunk/etc/apps Python script by postgres or splunkd (CVE-2026-20253 RCE primitive) AIInstallation High
Detects the arbitrary file-write primitive of the CVE-2026-20253 exploit chain: the PostgreSQL sidecar process writing or overwriting Python scripts under /opt/splunk/etc/apps/ — specifically targets the watchTowr-named payload location /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_secure_gateway/bin/ssg_enable_modular_input.py. Legitimate Splunk apps are NEVER modified by postgres. Rationale: Pivots on the exact attacker-controlled file-write target named in the watchTowr writeup: /opt/splunk/etc/apps/splunk_secure_gateway/bin/ssg_enable_modular_input.py. The combination of (path under /opt/splunk/etc/apps/) + (.py) + (postgres OR splunkd as writer) is extremely specific — postgres has no legitimate reason to write Splunk app Python scripts. Cross-checked against watchTowr Labs technical breakdown. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/ • https://advisory.splunk.com/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1574
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Splunk app installation via `splunk install app <bundle>` (writer would be splunkd not postgres — refine if needed)
  • Splunk version upgrade replacing built-in apps (writer is splunkd, not postgres)
  • Admin manually editing scripts via SSH (writer is bash/vi, AccountName is a real user, not postgres service account)
  • Configuration management tool (Ansible/Puppet) deploying custom Splunk apps
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName == "splunkd" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install app", "upgrade", "btool"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Pull the written file content and hash. Compare against the legitimate version from Splunk's release tarball. Check the writing process's parent chain — postgres writing a Python file is never legitimate. Pull contemporaneous web logs for /v1/postgres/recovery/* hits from same host. 2) CONTAIN — Isolate the Splunk host from the network. Stop splunkd before the modular input fires the payload. Snapshot the modified file and PostgreSQL transaction log. Restore the .py file from a clean backup or release tarball. 3) HUNT — Search for splunkd or postgres child processes (UC3) post-write. Check for outbound C2 from the host to attacker infrastructure. Review .pgpass access (UC4). Look for similar file-writes on every Splunk Enterprise host running < 10.2.4 / 10.0.7.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "/opt/splunk/etc/apps/"
| where FileName endswith ".py"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("postgres", "splunkd", "sh", "bash", "dash")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath has "/opt/splunk/etc/apps/"
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "py" or TargetFileName endswith ".py"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("postgres", "splunkd", "sh", "bash", "dash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Splunk App Python Script Overwritten by PostgreSQL or splunkd (CVE-2026-20253 RCE)
id: 8e2a91b4-7c3d-4f8a-b1e6-3f5d9c2e7a8b
description: Detects the arbitrary-file-write primitive of CVE-2026-20253. The PostgreSQL sidecar lo_export function is abused to overwrite a Python script under /opt/splunk/etc/apps/, most notably ssg_enable_modular_input.py, which Splunk subsequently executes — yielding code execution under the Splunk service account.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/critical-splunk-enterprise-flaw-lets.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1574
  - attack.persistence
  - cve.2026.20253
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: '/opt/splunk/etc/apps/'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.py'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/postgres'
      - '/splunkd'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/dash'
  condition: selection_path and selection_proc
falsepositives:
  - Splunk app installation via splunk install app (legit splunkd-driven writes during admin-initiated upgrade)
level: critical
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) @file.path:*/opt/splunk/etc/apps/* @file.path:*.py @process.name:(postgres OR splunkd OR sh OR bash OR dash)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten regex("/opt/splunk/etc/apps/", field=TargetFileName) TargetFileName=/\.py$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(postgres|splunkd|bash|sh|dash)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.action) as actions values(Filesystem.process_name) as procs from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="/opt/splunk/etc/apps/*" Filesystem.file_name="*.py") AND (Filesystem.process_name="postgres" OR Filesystem.process_name="splunkd" OR Filesystem.process_name="sh" OR Filesystem.process_name="bash") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.action) as actions values(Filesystem.process_name) as procs from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="/opt/splunk/etc/apps/*" Filesystem.file_name="*.py") AND (Filesystem.process_name="postgres" OR Filesystem.process_name="splunkd" OR Filesystem.process_name="sh" OR Filesystem.process_name="bash") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
splunkd or PostgreSQL spawning shell/interpreter after CVE-2026-20253 exploit AIInstallation High
Detects the post-exploitation code-execution stage of CVE-2026-20253: the embedded PostgreSQL sidecar or splunkd spawning a shell or scripting interpreter. Once the malicious Python script lands under /opt/splunk/etc/apps/, Splunk executes it under the service account — the resulting shell process is the cleanest behavioural signal. Rationale: Pivots on the article's named victim process (splunkd executes the planted Python script) AND its embedded postgres sidecar (the direct executor of lo_export's payload). Legitimate splunkd scripted inputs almost never invoke /dev/tcp redirection, base64-decoded payloads, or shells running out of /tmp or /dev/shm — the command-line tokens chosen here are reverse-shell-only patterns. Cross-checked watchTowr writeup confirming RCE lands as Splunk-user-context code execution. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.006 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Splunk modular inputs that legitimately use Python scripts (e.g. Add-on for AWS, ServiceNow modular inputs) — won't have reverse-shell tokens
  • Splunk admins running `splunk cmd btool` or `splunk cmd python` from terminal — parent would be a login shell, not splunkd
  • Custom scripted inputs that legitimately call curl/wget to internal API endpoints
  • Splunk diag bundle generation invoking helper binaries
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("splunkd -p ", "splunkd start", "splunk cmd btool", "splunk-launch.conf"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Pull the full command line; the /dev/tcp/ string reveals the C2 IP/port. Identify the executing Splunk user (AccountName / InitiatingProcessAccountName) and the parent chain back to splunkd. 2) CONTAIN — Kill the spawned shell PID. Stop splunkd. Block the C2 IP at the network edge. Snapshot the host for forensics including /opt/splunk/etc/apps/ and PostgreSQL data directory. 3) HUNT — Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId tracing the reverse-shell connection and any subsequent outbound C2. Search for the same source IP that hit /v1/postgres/recovery endpoints (UC1). Check the entire Splunk fleet for the modified .py file (UC2) and run UC4 to detect .pgpass reads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("splunkd", "splunkd.exe", "postgres", "postgres.exe", "splunk")
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "zsh", "ksh", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh", "python", "python3", "perl", "ruby", "nc", "ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/", "bash -i", "/tmp/", "/dev/shm/", "nc -", "curl ", "wget ", "base64 -d", "python -c", "perl -e", "sh -i", "-RemoteShell")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("splunkd", "postgres", "splunk")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh", "bash", "dash", "zsh", "ksh", "powershell", "pwsh", "python", "python3", "perl", "ruby", "nc", "ncat")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/", "bash -i", "/tmp/", "/dev/shm/", "nc -", "curl ", "wget ", "base64 -d", "python -c", "perl -e", "sh -i")

title: Splunk Service Process Spawning Shell or Interpreter (CVE-2026-20253 Post-Exploit)
id: 4f8c1e9d-3a7b-4d2e-9c1a-2b6e5d3f8a4c
description: Detects splunkd or its embedded postgres sidecar spawning a Unix shell or scripting interpreter with command-line indicators of a reverse shell or downloader. This is the most reliable host-side signal of successful CVE-2026-20253 exploitation.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/critical-splunk-enterprise-flaw-lets.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1059.006
  - attack.execution
  - cve.2026.20253
logsource:
  product: linux
  category: process_creation
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/splunkd'
      - '/postgres'
      - '/splunk'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
      - '/ruby'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/dev/tcp/'
      - 'bash -i'
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
      - 'base64 -d'
      - 'python -c'
      - 'perl -e'
      - 'sh -i'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
  - Splunk scripted inputs legitimately invoking Python or shell scripts (refine by excluding known app paths)
  - Admin troubleshooting via splunk cmd
level: critical
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:(splunkd OR postgres OR splunk) @process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash OR zsh OR python OR python3 OR perl OR ruby OR nc OR ncat) @process.command_line:(*"/dev/tcp/"* OR *"bash -i"* OR *"/tmp/"* OR *"/dev/shm/"* OR *"base64 -d"* OR *"python -c"* OR *"perl -e"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(splunkd|postgres|splunk)$/i
| ImageFileName=/(\/sh|\/bash|\/dash|\/zsh|\/python3?|\/perl|\/ruby|\/nc|\/ncat)$/i
| regex("(/dev/tcp/|bash -i|/tmp/|/dev/shm/|base64 -d|python -c|perl -e|sh -i)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdlines values(Processes.parent_process) as parents from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="splunkd" OR Processes.parent_process_name="postgres") (Processes.process_name="sh" OR Processes.process_name="bash" OR Processes.process_name="dash" OR Processes.process_name="python" OR Processes.process_name="python3" OR Processes.process_name="perl" OR Processes.process_name="ruby" OR Processes.process_name="nc") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(cmdlines, "/dev/tcp/|bash -i|/tmp/|curl |wget |base64 -d|python -c|perl -e|nc -") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmdlines values(Processes.parent_process) as parents from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name="splunkd" OR Processes.parent_process_name="postgres") (Processes.process_name="sh" OR Processes.process_name="bash" OR Processes.process_name="dash" OR Processes.process_name="python" OR Processes.process_name="python3" OR Processes.process_name="perl" OR Processes.process_name="ruby" OR Processes.process_name="nc") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(cmdlines, "/dev/tcp/|bash -i|/tmp/|curl |wget |base64 -d|python -c|perl -e|nc -") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Read or write of Splunk .pgpass at /opt/splunk/var/packages/data/postgres/.pgpass AIExploitation Medium
Detects access to the PostgreSQL password file referenced explicitly by the CVE-2026-20253 exploit — /opt/splunk/var/packages/data/postgres/.pgpass — which the attacker points the `passfile` argument at to authenticate as the postgres_admin user during the /restore exploitation step. Reads or writes to this file outside of splunkd init are highly suspicious. Rationale: Pivots on the exact .pgpass path string named in the watchTowr writeup (/opt/splunk/var/packages/data/postgres/.pgpass) and the article body. The attack uniquely requires touching this file via the passfile argument to authenticate as postgres_admin during /restore. Only splunkd itself should ever touch this file in normal operation — non-splunkd readers are a high-fidelity indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://labs.watchtowr.com/
ATT&CKT1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Splunk admin inspecting the file with cat/less/vi during troubleshooting
  • Backup software (Veeam agent, restic, borg) reading the entire /opt/splunk tree
  • Splunk diag bundle generation (splunkd subprocesses)
  • Configuration management tool (Ansible/Puppet) auditing file presence
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "restic", "borg", "tar", "rsync", "diag"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Identify the process and user that accessed the file. Correlate with web requests to /v1/postgres/recovery/restore from the previous 5 minutes (UC1). If the writer is postgres rather than splunkd, this is near-certain exploitation. 2) CONTAIN — Stop splunkd, isolate host. Rotate the postgres_admin credential and any other secrets in the .pgpass file. Snapshot the host. 3) HUNT — Pivot to UC2 (Python script writes under apps), UC3 (splunkd/postgres spawning shells). Across the fleet, find every Splunk Enterprise instance below 10.2.4 / 10.0.7 and check for unexpected .pgpass access in the last 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has "/opt/splunk/var/packages/data/postgres/"
| where FileName == ".pgpass"
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("splunkd", "splunk"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has "/opt/splunk/var/packages/data/postgres/"
| where TargetFileName == ".pgpass"
| where not(ActingProcessName in~ ("splunkd", "splunk"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

400+ AUR Packages Hijacked: What the “Atomic Arch” Campaign Means for Supply-Chain Security

StepSecurity
2026-06-13 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On June 11th 2026, security researchers and the Arch Linux community disclosed a large-scale supply-chain attack against the Arch User Repository (AUR). Attackers hijacked more than 400 community packages and turned them into a malware delivery network. While the immediate blast radius is limited to Arch Linux systems, the campaign is a textbook example of how modern attackers compromise developers and CI infrastructure by abusing trust in open-source ecosystems.

ATT&CKT1190 T1539 T1555.003
Domainstemp.sh github.com/fardewoak/nodejs-argo
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
