Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or SHA1 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or MD5 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or SHA1 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40") or MD5 in~ ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b", "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-21509", "CVE-2023-50224")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-21509", "CVE-2023-50224")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Budibase CVE-2026-48150: POST /api/public/v1/roles/assign with global builder/admin grant in body · [LLM] Budibase: API key minted via /api/global/self/api_key then /api/public/v1/roles/assign within 5m

Budibase CVE-2026-48150: POST /api/public/v1/roles/assign with global builder/admin grant in body AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP POSTs to the vulnerable Budibase public-API role-assignment endpoint that carry `builder:true` or `admin:true` in the JSON body — the exact payload shape that triggers CVE-2026-48150 mass-assignment. Article-specific: the controller spreads `assignmentProps` straight into the SDK, so the body content is the high-fidelity tell. Rationale: Endpoint path (`/api/public/v1/roles/assign`), method (POST), and body keys (`"builder":true` / `"admin":true`) are taken verbatim from the article's PoC curl. Both URL-encoded and raw forms covered for reverse-proxy logs that record query strings differently. Defender KQL left empty — body inspection is not in DeviceNetworkEvents. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2g39-332f-68p9
ATT&CKT1068 T1190 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate tenant admin promoting a new builder via the public API (filter by SourceUserName allow-list)
  • Budibase upgrade scripts replaying recorded admin requests against a staging tenant
  • Penetration test / red team exercise reproducing the PoC for the same advisory
  • Automation that grants global-builder to service accounts post-onboarding
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("svc-budibase-onboard", "svc-budibase-scim") | where RequestClientApplication !has "BudibaseAdminConsole"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SourceIP + SourceUserName, look up the calling identity in Budibase admin console. Confirm whether the caller had global-builder or global-admin BEFORE the request — if not, treat as confirmed exploit. 2) Contain: revoke the API key (`/api/global/self/api_key` rotate), unset `builder.global` / `admin.global` on every userId in the request body, force-logout all sessions for the caller and any granted users, block the SourceIP at the ingress. 3) Hunt: pivot on SourceIP and SourceUserName for the prior 30 days against all `/api/public/v1/*` calls; enumerate every user whose `builder.global` or `admin.global` is currently true and verify against your role-baseline; check audit logs for SCIM/OIDC config edits made by the granted accounts.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where Message has_any ("\"builder\":true", "\"admin\":true", "builder%22%3Atrue", "admin%22%3Atrue")
    or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("\"builder\":true", "\"admin\":true")
    or DeviceCustomString2 has_any ("\"builder\":true", "\"admin\":true")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, RequestContext, Message, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Budibase audit log: builder.global / admin.global granted to user by non-global caller AIActions on Objectives High
Parses Budibase server stdout / audit lines forwarded as Syslog for the role-assignment mutation introduced by CVE-2026-48150. Flags lines where the SDK wrote `builder.global=true` or `admin.global=true` on a user account, then extracts the target userId and grant scope so the analyst can correlate with the caller identity. Rationale: Audit-log strings (`/api/public/v1/roles/assign`, `builder.global`, `admin.global`, `x-budibase-api-key`, `us_` userId prefix, `app_` appId prefix) all come straight from the article's controller/SDK code paths and PoC curl. Sentinel `extend` columns are created from the raw `SyslogMessage`, not referenced as table columns. Defender KQL left blank — Budibase audit logs do not ship to Defender XDR tables. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh
ATT&CKT1098 T1068
Data sourcesChange.Account_Management
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tenant admin doing legitimate role assignment via the public API (caller will already be global-admin)
  • Budibase Enterprise migration scripts seeding role state on a fresh install
  • Internal IaC / provisioning workflow that grants global-builder to a CI service account
Suppression filter
| where CallerApiKey !in ("<known-svc-key-hash1>", "<known-svc-key-hash2>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract `TargetUserId` and `CallerApiKey` from the alert. Look up the caller's role state at T-5min in Budibase admin — if `builder.global=false` and `admin.global=false` with `builder.apps` set, exploit is confirmed. 2) Contain: revoke caller's API key, reset target user's role to the baseline (re-apply `builder.apps` scope, unset `global`), force-logout all granted users. 3) Hunt: search Syslog for any other `roles/assign` writes by the same `CallerApiKey` or `AppIdHeader` in the prior 30 days; pivot on `TargetUserId` to find any SCIM / OIDC / datasource changes those users made post-grant.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has_any ("budibase", "node", "budibase-worker", "budibase-apps")
| where SyslogMessage has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("\"builder\":true", "\"admin\":true", "builder.global", "admin.global")
| extend TargetUserId = extract(@"us_[a-z0-9]+", 0, SyslogMessage)
| extend GrantedScope = case(
    SyslogMessage has "admin.global" or SyslogMessage has "\"admin\":true", "admin.global",
    SyslogMessage has "builder.global" or SyslogMessage has "\"builder\":true", "builder.global",
    "unknown")
| extend CallerApiKey = extract(@"x-budibase-api-key[^a-f0-9]*([a-f0-9]{16,})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend AppIdHeader = extract(@"app_[a-z0-9]+", 0, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, ProcessName, GrantedScope, TargetUserId, CallerApiKey, AppIdHeader, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(nodejs OR docker) "/api/public/v1/roles/assign" ("builder.global" OR "admin.global" OR "builder\":true" OR "admin\":true") @service:budibase*
APPLICATION

Budibase: rapid bulk POSTs to /api/public/v1/roles/assign from single source AIActions on Objectives Medium
Catches mass-assignment abuse where an attacker sweeps multiple users (or repeatedly flips builder→admin on themselves, per article PoC step 4) via repeated calls to the vulnerable endpoint. Threshold tuned to the article's pattern where Alice issued one grant-builder + one grant-admin in quick succession. Rationale: Article's PoC shows two consecutive grants from one identity (Alice→victim, then Alice→Alice). A workspace-scoped builder making >3 POSTs to this endpoint in 5 minutes has no legitimate use case — the public API is not normally driven from manual operator workflows. Threshold > 3 over 5m chosen to catch the PoC pattern while tolerating one legitimate scripted promotion. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh
ATT&CKT1068 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SCIM bulk-sync after IdP group change replays many role assignments
  • Tenant migration / IaC apply that grants role to many users at once
  • Budibase Enterprise onboarding script seeding builders for a new workspace
  • Load-test or CI smoke test against staging tenant
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<scim-svc-ip>", "<ci-svc-ip>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate every userId in the bursting calls' bodies — these are the privilege grant targets. Cross-reference SourceIP against known CI / SCIM service ranges. 2) Contain: revoke the caller's API key; for every targeted userId run the inverse SDK call to unset `builder.global` / `admin.global` and restore `builder.apps` scope. 3) Hunt: pivot on the SourceIP and SourceUserName for the prior 30 days to find recon (`GET /api/global/users`) or earlier suspicious public-API usage; check whether any newly-elevated users created datasources / automations / SCIM-OIDC config changes after the burst.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| summarize PostCount = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            DistinctBodies = dcount(Message),
            DistinctUserAgents = dcount(RequestClientApplication),
            SampleBody = any(Message)
            by SourceIP, SourceUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where PostCount > 3
| extend DurationSec = datetime_diff('second', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| order by PostCount desc

Budibase: API key minted via /api/global/self/api_key then /api/public/v1/roles/assign within 5m AIExploitation High
Reproduces the exact two-step chain from the CVE-2026-48150 PoC (step 2 mints the key, step 3 uses it to escalate). Joining the mint event to the assign event narrows on attacker tradecraft — the legitimate operator path uses long-lived keys, not key-minted-then-used. Rationale: Two-step chain (`GET /api/global/self/api_key` → `POST /api/public/v1/roles/assign`) is the exact tradecraft documented in the PoC (steps 2 and 3). 5-minute window matches the human-operator pace shown in the article and rules out long-lived legitimate keys. Datadog query is OR-joined for use as a rule-level correlation; not a single search-bar match. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6xp4-cf37-ppjh
ATT&CKT1098.001 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator setting up new automation pulls a self-key then immediately tests it against the public API
  • Internal onboarding tooling that scripts both calls back-to-back for new builders
  • Pen test / red team validating CVE-2026-48150 against a tenant
Suppression filter
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("svc-budibase-onboard", "svc-budibase-ci")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the caller from the join, verify whether they already had global-builder/global-admin before `KeyMintTime` — if not, this is the CVE chain. 2) Contain: revoke the minted API key, unset elevated flags on every userId named in the assign request body, force-logout the caller and granted users. 3) Hunt: scan the prior 30 days for the same SourceIP/SourceUserName hitting `/api/global/self/api_key`; pivot on the minted key prefix in subsequent public-API calls to find post-escalation reconnaissance or datasource credential reads.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMinutes = 5;
let KeyMints = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where RequestURL has "/api/global/self/api_key"
    | where RequestMethod =~ "GET"
    | project KeyMintTime = TimeGenerated, MintSourceIP = SourceIP, MintSourceUser = SourceUserName, MintUA = RequestClientApplication;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RequestURL has "/api/public/v1/roles/assign"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| join kind=inner KeyMints on $left.SourceIP == $right.MintSourceIP
| where TimeGenerated between (KeyMintTime .. KeyMintTime + WindowMinutes * 1m)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, KeyMintTime)
| project KeyMintTime, AssignTime = TimeGenerated, DelaySec, SourceIP, SourceUserName, MintSourceUser, MintUA, AssignUA = RequestClientApplication, RequestURL, RequestMethod, Message
| order by AssignTime desc

China-Linked Hackers Backdoored Linux Login Software to Hide for Nearly a Decade

The Hacker News
2026-06-12 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Instead of hiding on the laptops and servers defenders watch most closely, a China-nexus group spent close to a decade hidden inside the Linux login system itself. Sygnia, which tracks the group as Velvet Ant, says it backdoored the PAM and OpenSSH components that decide who is allowed to sign in, planting its access where ordinary cleanup could not reach it. The network it targeted had no

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Internet-facing web service spawning interactive SSH into management subnet · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Unauthorized write to Linux PAM authentication module (pam_unix.so swap) · [LLM] Unauthorized modification of OpenSSH sshd or ssh client binary · [LLM] First-seen pam_unix.so / sshd / ssh binary hash in Linux fleet
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations

Unauthorized write to Linux PAM authentication module (pam_unix.so swap) AIInstallation High
Detects file creation/modification of pam_unix.so (or sibling PAM modules) by any process other than the system package manager. Velvet Ant's Operation Highland replaced this exact module with 9 backdoored builds that accepted a magic password and logged real credentials — direct swap is the highest-fidelity persistence pivot in the campaign. Rationale: Article + Sygnia blog explicitly name pam_unix.so as the swapped module with 9 backdoored variants discovered. File-write to canonical PAM module paths by a non-package-manager process is a direct hit on the documented TTP and effectively unfalsifiable without legitimate package activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/china-nexus-group-hid-in-linux-login-system-for-nearly-a-decade
ATT&CKT1556.003 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro security update outside the maintained package-manager allowlist (e.g. manually invoked 'install' on a downloaded .deb via curl|sh)
  • Configuration management agent (Ansible/Salt/Puppet) deploying a custom or in-house PAM module under a non-standard process name
  • Container-image build process writing PAM modules during image construction
  • System administrator manually reinstalling pam package via 'apt-get install --reinstall' under sudo from interactive shell
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","cfengine") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--reinstall","makepkg","rpmbuild"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — extract SHA256 of the written .so; compare against distro package hash via 'rpm -V pam' or 'dpkg --verify libpam-modules'; review process tree of InitiatingProcessFileName and its parent; check whether the host had a sanctioned change window. 2) Contain — isolate the host; snapshot /lib*/security/ and /etc/pam.d/ for forensics; revoke and rotate every credential used to SSH to or sudo on the host within the lookback (article: credentials captured at login). 3) Hunt — fan out the SHA256 across the Linux fleet; pull sshd and ssh binary hashes from the same host; hunt outbound DNS/TCP from sshd-context processes for any kill-switch beacon.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"/lib/security/", @"/lib64/security/", @"/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/", @"/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/", @"/usr/lib64/security/")
| where FileName startswith "pam_" and FileName endswith ".so"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dpkg","dpkg-deb","apt","apt-get","aptitude","unattended-upgrade","yum","dnf","rpm","zypper","pacman","ldconfig","snapd","snap")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, MD5, PreviousFileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/lib/security/","/lib64/security/","/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/","/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/security/","/usr/lib64/security/")
| where TargetFileName startswith "pam_" and TargetFileName endswith ".so"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("dpkg","dpkg-deb","apt","apt-get","aptitude","unattended-upgrade","yum","dnf","rpm","zypper","pacman","ldconfig","snapd","snap")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthorized modification of OpenSSH sshd or ssh client binary AIInstallation High
Detects write or replacement of the canonical OpenSSH binaries (/usr/sbin/sshd, /usr/bin/ssh) outside of package-manager updates. Operation Highland modified these binaries to log credentials and every command typed with a hidden switch to silence logging, making any uncontrolled write to them campaign-defining. Rationale: Article + Sygnia state sshd/ssh were altered to log credentials and typed commands with a hidden disable switch. Detecting file writes to the canonical OpenSSH paths by anything other than the package manager is a direct, low-FP hit on the documented persistence method. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/china-nexus-group-hid-in-linux-login-system-for-nearly-a-decade

sshd writing to non-standard files (credential-capture log artifact) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the sshd process writing to file paths outside its expected runtime set (PID file, audit/syslog sockets, sftp transfer targets). The Operation Highland sshd backdoor recorded every credential and typed command to a hidden file; any file-write originating from sshd to /tmp, /var/tmp, /dev/shm, /etc, or a non-standard path under /var is the artefact. Rationale: Article: Operation Highland sshd 'logging credentials and every command typed, with a hidden switch to turn that logging off when needed.' The capture file has to land somewhere on disk. sshd's expected write set is small (PID, syslog forwards, user .ssh, sftp transfers) — anything else from sshd is a credential-capture candidate. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/
ATT&CKT1056.001 T1003.008 T1556.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • sftp-internal subsystem inside sshd writing user-uploaded files to non-/home destinations
  • PAM session module writing motd/lastlog timestamps via sshd context to a vendor-custom path
  • Container-friendly sshd builds that write a runtime socket to /tmp under a non-standard name
  • Custom sshd ChrootDirectory configurations placing user data outside /home
  • Local PAM module from an EDR/UEBA agent writing audit breadcrumbs into /var/lib/<vendor>/
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/var/lib/" and FolderPath has_any ("crowdstrike","sentinelone","defender","qualys","rapid7"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — read the written file (cat / xxd first bytes) to confirm credential-style content (usernames, plaintext passwords, typed commands); cross-check sshd binary SHA256 against the distro package. 2) Contain — isolate host; copy and quarantine the capture file for forensics; replace sshd from verified package source; force password + key rotation for every account that authenticated to the host since the file's first-seen timestamp. 3) Hunt — pivot on the file path across the Linux fleet; check for matching pam_unix.so anomalies; review egress from sshd-context to identify out-of-band exfil of the capture file.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sshd"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/bin/")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where not (FolderPath in~ ("/var/run/","/run/","/var/log/","/var/empty/sshd/","/var/lib/sss/") )
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/home/" and FolderPath contains "/.ssh/")
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/root/.ssh/")
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/tmp/ssh-")
| where FileName !in~ ("sshd.pid","auth.log","secure","lastlog","wtmp","btmp","utmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RequestAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName =~ "sshd"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith "/var/run/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/run/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/log/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/empty/sshd/" or TargetFilePath startswith "/var/lib/sss/")
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith "/home/" and TargetFilePath contains "/.ssh/")
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith "/root/.ssh/")
| where not (TargetFilePath startswith "/tmp/ssh-")
| where TargetFileName !in~ ("sshd.pid","auth.log","secure","lastlog","wtmp","btmp","utmp")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(PATH OR SYSCALL) @process.executable.path:(/usr/sbin/sshd OR /usr/bin/sshd) @auditd.syscall:(open OR openat OR write OR creat OR rename) -@file.path:(/var/run/sshd.pid OR /run/sshd.pid OR /var/log/auth.log OR /var/log/secure OR /var/log/wtmp OR /var/log/btmp OR /var/log/lastlog OR /var/log/utmp OR /var/empty/sshd/* OR /home/*/.ssh/* OR /root/.ssh/* OR /tmp/ssh-* OR /var/lib/sss/*)

| NOT TargetFileName=/\/(var\/run\/sshd\.pid|run\/sshd\.pid|var\/log\/(auth\.log|secure|wtmp|btmp|lastlog|utmp)|home\/[^\/]+\/\.ssh\/.*|root\/\.ssh\/.*|tmp\/ssh-.*|var\/empty\/sshd\/.*|var\/lib\/sss\/.*)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, UserName], function=count())
| count > 0
ENDPOINT

Internet-facing web service spawning interactive SSH into management subnet AIDelivery High
Detects a web server process (httpd, nginx, apache2, tomcat, php-fpm, node, java app server) spawning ssh/scp/sftp/sshpass to an internal RFC1918 destination — the exact pivot Sygnia attributes to Operation Highland, where an internet-facing web server was used as a bridge to open remote sessions deep inside an air-gapped segment. Rationale: Article: 'used other disguised tools and an internet-facing web server as a bridge, passing commands through it to open remote sessions deep inside the segment that had no direct internet access.' A web-server parent spawning ssh/scp/sftp/socat at all is rare in production; targeting RFC1918 makes it the pivot signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/china-nexus-group-hid-in-linux-login-system-for-nearly-a-decade
ATT&CKT1190 T1133 T1021.004 T1090.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD agent embedded in a web tier (e.g. Jenkins runner under tomcat) legitimately scp-ing build artefacts to internal hosts
  • Deploy hook in a PHP app calling 'ssh deploy@internal' as part of release automation
  • Healthcheck plugin shelling 'nc -zv internal-db 5432' from haproxy
  • Log-shipping script invoked from nginx error handler that uses scp to push debug bundles
  • Backup wrapper inside a java app server initiating scp to an internal backup target
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("jenkins","deploy","gitlab-runner","awx","rundeck") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("deploy","backup","rsync")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the web server access log for the same minute and identify the request path that triggered the spawn (webshell signature); inspect the SSH destination IP and the credential/key used; check whether the web server has a documented automation parent. 2) Contain — kill active ssh/socat session; block egress from web tier to management subnet at host firewall; quarantine any webshell artefact found in the web root; rotate keys/passwords for the target account. 3) Hunt — fan-out same parent→child pairing across other internet-facing hosts; pivot on the destination internal IP to identify what the attacker reached; check the destination for pam_unix.so / sshd hash anomalies.
let WebParents = dynamic(["httpd","nginx","apache2","tomcat","java","node","php-fpm","php-cgi","uwsgi","gunicorn","caddy","lighttpd","haproxy"]);
let PivotTools = dynamic(["ssh","sshpass","scp","sftp","plink","autossh","socat","ncat","nc"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (WebParents)
| where FileName in~ (PivotTools)
| extend RfcTarget = extract(@"(?:^|\s)(?:-[a-zA-Z]\s+)?(?:[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+@)?((?:10\.|172\.(?:1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.)\d+\.\d+\.\d+|(?:10\.|172\.(?:1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.)[0-9.]+)", 1, ProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(RfcTarget) or ProcessCommandLine has_any (".internal",".corp",".local",".lan",".intranet")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, RfcTarget, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let WebParents = dynamic(["httpd","nginx","apache2","tomcat","java","node","php-fpm","php-cgi","uwsgi","gunicorn","caddy","lighttpd","haproxy"]);
let PivotTools = dynamic(["ssh","sshpass","scp","sftp","plink","autossh","socat","ncat","nc"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName in~ (WebParents)
| where ActingProcessName in~ (PivotTools)
| extend RfcTarget = extract(@"(?:^|\s)(?:-[a-zA-Z]\s+)?(?:[A-Za-z0-9_\-]+@)?((?:10\.|172\.(?:1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\.|192\.168\.)[0-9.]+)", 1, ActingProcessCommandLine)
| where isnotempty(RfcTarget) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (".internal",".corp",".local",".lan",".intranet")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, RfcTarget
| order by TimeGenerated desc

source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:(httpd OR nginx OR apache2 OR tomcat OR java OR node OR php-fpm OR php-cgi OR uwsgi OR gunicorn OR caddy OR lighttpd OR haproxy) @process.name:(ssh OR sshpass OR scp OR sftp OR plink OR autossh OR socat OR ncat OR nc) (@process.command_line:*10.* OR @process.command_line:*172.16.* OR @process.command_line:*172.17.* OR @process.command_line:*172.18.* OR @process.command_line:*172.19.* OR @process.command_line:*172.2* OR @process.command_line:*172.30.* OR @process.command_line:*172.31.* OR @process.command_line:*192.168.* OR @process.command_line:*.internal* OR @process.command_line:*.corp* OR @process.command_line:*.local* OR @process.command_line:*.lan*)

| regex("(10\\.|172\\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[01])\\.|192\\.168\\.|\\.internal|\\.corp|\\.local|\\.lan|\\.intranet)", field=CommandLine)

First-seen pam_unix.so / sshd / ssh binary hash in Linux fleet AIInstallation Medium
Anti-baseline hunting query: surfaces SHA256 values of pam_unix.so, sshd, ssh, scp, sftp that appear in the recent window but were never observed in the 60-day baseline. Velvet Ant built 9 distinct compile-variants of pam_unix.so per host — a fresh hash on a long-stable binary is the canonical indicator regardless of how it got there. Rationale: Article + Sygnia: 9 distinct compile-variants of pam_unix.so per Operation Highland host. Hash-anti-baseline catches the variant regardless of write path; works even when the swap predates monitoring (because the new hash will eventually appear in execution/load telemetry). Cross-checked against: • https://www.sygnia.co/blog/operation-highland-velvet-ant/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/china-nexus-group-hid-in-linux-login-system-for-nearly-a-decade
ATT&CKT1554 T1556.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Distro security update introducing a new openssh-server build (legitimate new hash, fleet-wide)
  • Newly onboarded host running a different distro version not present in baseline
  • libpam-modules upgrade pushing a new pam_unix.so build
  • In-house custom-compiled OpenSSH rollout under a change ticket
  • Hardened-image refresh from golden image producing new but legitimate hashes
Suppression filter
| where not (FirstSeen > ago(48h) and HostCount > 100)
Response runbook
1) Triage — correlate the new hash against the package metadata on the host ('rpm -V', 'dpkg -V libpam-modules openssh-server') and against the distro vendor's signed package hash; if the hash is unaccounted for, treat as suspect. 2) Contain — isolate the host; preserve binary + memory; restore from verified package mirror; rotate credentials used since the binary first appeared. 3) Hunt — pivot on the unaccounted hash across the fleet to find all infected hosts; cross-check whether the same hosts also have anomalous sshd or pam_unix.so; review egress from those hosts during their first-seen window.
let Lookback = 60d;
let Recent = 7d;
let AuthBinaries = dynamic(["sshd","ssh","scp","sftp","ssh-keygen","ssh-agent"]);
let BaselineExec = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where FileName in~ (AuthBinaries) and FolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/bin/")
    | summarize by SHA256, FileName;
let RecentExec = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Recent)
    | where FileName in~ (AuthBinaries) and FolderPath in~ ("/usr/sbin/","/usr/bin/")
    | summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), HostCount = dcount(DeviceId), AnyHost = any(DeviceName), AnyCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by SHA256, FileName, FolderPath;
let NewExec = RecentExec | join kind=leftanti BaselineExec on SHA256, FileName | extend Kind = "sshd/ssh exec";
let BaselineLoad = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where FileName == "pam_unix.so"
    | summarize by SHA256, FileName;
let RecentLoad = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(Recent)
    | where FileName == "pam_unix.so"
    | summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), HostCount = dcount(DeviceId), AnyHost = any(DeviceName), AnyCmd = "" by SHA256, FileName, FolderPath;
let NewLoad = RecentLoad | join kind=leftanti BaselineLoad on SHA256, FileName | extend Kind = "pam_unix.so load";
union NewExec, NewLoad
| order by FirstSeen desc
let Lookback = 60d;
let Recent = 7d;
let AuthBinaries = dynamic(["sshd","ssh","scp","sftp","ssh-keygen","ssh-agent"]);
let Baseline = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(Recent))
    | where ActingProcessName in~ (AuthBinaries)
    | summarize by Hash = tostring(SHA256), ActingProcessName;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Recent)
| where ActingProcessName in~ (AuthBinaries)
| extend Hash = tostring(SHA256)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on Hash, ActingProcessName
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), HostCount = dcount(DvcHostname), AnyHost = any(DvcHostname), AnyCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine) by Hash, ActingProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.executable.path:(/usr/sbin/sshd OR /usr/bin/sshd OR /usr/bin/ssh OR /usr/sbin/ssh OR /usr/bin/scp OR /usr/bin/sftp OR /usr/bin/ssh-keygen OR /usr/bin/ssh-agent) @process.executable.hash:*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(usr\/sbin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/ssh|usr\/sbin\/ssh|usr\/bin\/scp|usr\/bin\/sftp|usr\/bin\/ssh-keygen|usr\/bin\/ssh-agent)$/i
| groupBy([SHA256HashData, ImageFileName], function={ min(_time, as=FirstSeen) | count(field=aid, distinct=true, as=HostCount) })
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(usr\/sbin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/sshd|usr\/bin\/ssh|usr\/sbin\/ssh|usr\/bin\/scp|usr\/bin\/sftp|usr\/bin\/ssh-keygen|usr\/bin\/ssh-agent)$/i _time<now()-7d | groupBy([SHA256HashData], function=count(as=BaselineCount))}, field=SHA256HashData, include=[BaselineCount], mode=left)
| BaselineCount=null
| sort(FirstSeen, order=desc)
ENDPOINT

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

            - 'wget '

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    selection_child:

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

| where Account !endswith "$"

Atomic Arch — pacman/makepkg post-install spawning npm install of atomic-lockfile AIInstallation High
Detects the install-time pivot of the Atomic Arch supply-chain campaign: a pacman/makepkg PKGBUILD post-install hook spawning npm or node to fetch the malicious atomic-lockfile package. The combination of an Arch package-build parent with an npm child referencing atomic-lockfile is specific to this campaign and absent from clean AUR installs. Rationale: atomic-lockfile is the named malicious npm package both IFIN and Sonatype identified as the second-stage payload of the Atomic Arch campaign. Pacman/makepkg are the only legitimate Arch package-build parents — they should never spawn npm referencing this string. Cross-checked with Sonatype's writeup on the AUR PKGBUILD post-install hook. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-400-arch-linux-packages-compromised-to-push-rootkit-infostealer/ • https://www.sonatype.com/blog • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.004 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate AUR maintainer publishing a benign package literally named atomic-lockfile or with that string in a dependency (none currently exist on npm)
  • Developer manually invoking npm install atomic-lockfile while researching this campaign
  • Security team running validation tests against the IOC
  • SBOM/dependency-audit tools that enumerate package names in logs
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","--audit-only")) and not(AccountName in~ ("securityresearch","detectiondev"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host installed an AUR package in the preceding 10 minutes via /var/log/pacman.log; identify the trojanized PKGBUILD owner and capture the SHA256 of the npm-dropped ELF. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the workstation from the network, kill the npm/node descendant process tree, and snapshot /tmp, ~/.npm, and ~/.cache for forensics before reimaging. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the developer's identity — rotate GitHub PATs, npm tokens, SSH keys, HashiCorp Vault tokens, and any Slack/Teams/Discord refresh tokens; search org-wide for other hosts installing the same AUR package name in the last 30 days; check DNS for temp.sh and any .onion resolution attempts from the affected subnet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("makepkg","pacman","bash","sh","zsh")
| where FileName has_any ("npm","node","pnpm","yarn","npx")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "atomic-lockfile"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "atomic-lockfile"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("makepkg","pacman","PKGBUILD")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("npm"," node ","pnpm","yarn","npx")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Atomic Arch — Pacman/Makepkg Spawns NPM Install of atomic-lockfile
id: 1a2b3c4d-5e6f-7081-9203-4567890abcde
description: Detects pacman or makepkg parent spawning an npm/node child that references the malicious atomic-lockfile package distributed by the Atomic Arch AUR supply-chain compromise.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-400-arch-linux-packages-compromised-to-push-rootkit-infostealer/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/12
tags:

  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - /makepkg
      - /pacman
      - /bash
      - /sh
      - /zsh
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - /npm
      - /node
      - /pnpm
      - /yarn
      - /npx
  selection_cmd:
    CommandLine|contains: atomic-lockfile
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(npm OR node OR pnpm OR yarn OR npx) @process.command_line:*atomic-lockfile*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/^(makepkg|pacman|bash|sh|zsh)$/i ImageFileName=/(npm|node|pnpm|yarn|npx)$/i
| regex("atomic-lockfile", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.parent_process) as parent_process values(Processes.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("makepkg","pacman","bash","sh","zsh") AND Processes.process_name IN ("npm","node","pnpm","yarn","npx") AND Processes.process="*atomic-lockfile*" by host Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Atomic Arch — ELF payload 'deps' written or executed under build/cache directories after AUR install AIInstallation High
Detects creation or execution of the ELF infostealer 'deps' dropped by the atomic-lockfile npm package, identified by its specific SHA256/MD5 and by the file name 'deps' landing in npm/build/cache directories shortly after an AUR install. This is the second-stage payload that performs credential harvesting. Rationale: SHA256 6144d433...3c98b and MD5 42b59fdb...bf40 are the article's pre-extracted IOCs for the 'deps' ELF infostealer. The filename 'deps' under npm/build/cache dirs is the secondary heuristic for variants of the same dropper where the hash has been recompiled. Cross-checked with the IFIN/Whanos report referenced in the article and MITRE T1204.002. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/over-400-arch-linux-packages-compromised-to-push-rootkit-infostealer/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate npm package shipping a binary called 'deps' as part of its build (some Go/Rust toolchains do this — verify by hash, not name alone)
  • Developer manually saving a hash-matching file from a research/sandbox
  • Security tooling that imports IOC sets into local test corpora
  • CI runners that bundle node_modules including binary helpers
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("/go/pkg/mod/","/cargo/registry/") and FileName == "deps")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the hash match; if name-only, compute and compare the actual SHA256 against the IOC. Pull pacman.log to identify the AUR package whose post-install triggered the npm fetch. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, terminate any running 'deps' process and its npm/node parent chain, preserve the binary and the npm cache for malware reverse-engineering. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep org-wide for the SHA256/MD5 IOCs and for any 'deps' ELF in user cache dirs; pivot on the maintainer alias on the affected AUR package and check if other PKGBUILDs from arojas, krisztinavarga, custodiatovar, or veramagalhaes were installed.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where SHA256 == "6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b"
   or MD5 == "42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40"
   or (FileName == "deps" and FolderPath has_any ("/.cache/", "/.npm/", "/build/", "/tmp/", "/node_modules/"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("6144d433f8a0316869877b5f834c801251bbb936e5f1577c5680878c7443c98b","42b59fdbe1b72895b2951412222ebf40")
   or (SyslogMessage has "name=\"deps\"" and SyslogMessage has_any ("/.cache/","/.npm/","/build/","/tmp/","/node_modules/"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostName, Facility, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
